Four Simsons

GeometryCirclesTriangles
Game: This is a picture, not a game: four lines and four circles drawn from four corners on one ring all cross at a single dot.
How to play: Drag A, B, C or D round the ring, or focus a corner and use the arrow keys. Tick the boxes to show the dots, circles and lines, then click a line to see why it is there.
Look for the math

Move a corner and the picture changes completely. Yet the four circles and four lines keep meeting in the same dot. What is that dot, and why can it never move away?

Four corners, four triangles

Four corners A, B, C, D on one circle make four triangles: BCD, CDA, DAB and ABC. Each triangle has an orthocenter HA (the meeting point of its three altitudes) and a circumcircle. Halfway between its orthocenter and its circumcenter sits the nine-point centre: N = (O + H) / 2. The nine-point circle centred there passes through the midpoints of the triangle's sides. The small dots in the picture are NA, NB, NC and ND.

Why the four circles meet

The four centres NANBNCND form a shape exactly like ABCD, only half its size. Its circumradius is therefore R/2, where R is the radius of the circle through A, B, C, D. Every triangle's nine-point circle also has radius R/2. Four equal circles whose centres lie R/2 from a common point must all pass through that point: the circumcenter of NANBNCND. That is the dot the circles share.

Why the four lines meet there too

Drop perpendiculars from A to the three sides of triangle BCD. When A lies on that triangle's circumcircle, the three feet lie in a row: that row is the Simson line of A. The shared dot is also the centre of the homothety that sends ABCD to the quadrilateral of the four orthocentres, so it is the midpoint of AHA, and likewise for B, C and D. A known property of the Simson line puts it through that midpoint. Click a line to see the triangle and the three feet that make it.

What the test found

The page's exact claim is that in a cyclic quadrilateral all eight objects concur. The logic test checks it independently on thousands of generated quadrilaterals, and compares every computed point with a second transcription of the applet's bytecode. It found no failure: the errors stay near 1e-9 times the size of the drawing. The page adds that for a non-cyclic quadrilateral the Simson lines turn into circles and the eight circles still concur; that was checked on hundreds of non-cyclic quadrilaterals too. The applet itself keeps its four corners on one circle and always draws a line through just two of the three feet, so this port does the same: the generalized circles are stated here, not drawn. Near a position where three corners almost line up, the construction is hidden rather than drawn with unreliable numbers.

Tick Simson lines, click the line of A, then drag A: the three perpendicular feet stay in a row while the triangle changes around them.
